why.answer: All three pass every rule the report holds a reply model to. By the report's own order, cheapest first, gpt-6-luna would lead, at $0.002 a conversation against $0.019. The owner approved gpt-6.1-terra in front of it on the builder's advice, which was a judgment more than a measurement: the gate that grades a reply checks rules and not depth, and a larger model was thought worth about 1.7 cents a conversation. gpt-6.1-terra's first drafts did pass more often here (83.3% against 75%), but that is two drafts of 24, within the spread of today's own runs (87.5% to 95.8%).
why.small: No small-job model passes every rule; the report lists the rules each one misses. The design says that the numbers then go to the owner, who approved gpt-6-luna on the builder's advice. It costs the same as today's model, gave a usable answer every time, kept the average lead score within 3 points of today's, named the nursing-home case rightly where today's model never does, and caught all six drafts that are wrong on purpose, where today's model caught two or three. What it misses is agreement with today's model on the case type and on a draft's first verdict, where it is the stricter of the two, and the four-second rule for grading a reply, which today's model misses too. Found after the choice: scoring leads, it made a claim that was years out of time a cold lead. The rule that such a claim is never a lead (scoreLead in auction.js) was added for that, on the owner's approval.
